Q807809.summary: At the centre of this five-part ivory leaf, an emperor on a rearing horse triumphs over a barbarian, while Earth bows at his foot and conquered peoples bring tribute below. In the upper panel, two flying angels hold up a medallion with the bust of a young, curly-haired Christ, raising his hand in blessing and holding a cross-sceptre. Christ reigns above while the emperor acts as his representative on earth.
facts: It is the only nearly complete surviving leaf of an imperial diptych; only the right-hand plaque is missing.
The emperor is usually identified as Justinian, though Anastasius has also been proposed; the prominence given to Christ blessing the emperor supports a Justinianic date.
The antiquary Peiresc gave it to Cardinal Francesco Barberini in 1625; the Louvre acquired it in 1899. Names of the kings of Austrasia are inscribed on the back.
Q807809.notes: Louvre dates it 525–550; worklist year 525 adjusted to the middle of the range.

cur:manuscripts-athelstan-psalter-christ.summary: At the top Christ sits enthroned in a mandorla holding a book and a cross, flanked by crowded ranks of angels labelled 'omnis chorus angelorum'; beneath, a band of prophets ('omnis chorus prophetarum') and, at the bottom, the apostles gathered around a central figure, probably the Virgin. The page presents the whole court of heaven gathered around Christ.
facts: The Athelstan Psalter is a 9th-century Carolingian psalter to which full-page miniatures were added in England in the 10th century; it is traditionally associated with King Æthelstan, and one of its leaves is now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Rawl. B 484).
The Latin inscriptions on the bands name the choirs of angels and of prophets.

cur:monumental-oberzell-raising-of-lazar.summary: Christ stands at the left with the apostles, raising his hand towards Lazarus, who stands wrapped in his grave-clothes within the tomb at the centre, while Martha or Mary kneels at Christ's feet and onlookers watch from the right. As the last scene of the cycle, beside the entrance, it forms the climax of the series of miracles.
facts: The eight miracle scenes on the nave walls of St George, Oberzell, were rediscovered under later plaster in 1880; they are dated either to about 900 (late Carolingian) or, in the prevailing view, to the late 10th century (Ottonian).

Apart from Müstair, St George is the only church north of the Alps in the former Empire to preserve so complete a cycle of early medieval wall painting; the sequence runs from the entrance along the north wall to the altar and back along the south wall, culminating in the Raising of Lazarus.
In each scene Christ, larger than the other figures, stands at the left with a gesture of blessing directed into the narrative, except in two scenes where he appears twice.

cur:monumental2-agacalti-ascension.summary: At the centre of the small cut-rock dome, Christ rises within a circular mandorla of concentric bands, borne up by angels whose wings spread around it, while the apostles stand in a ring of pale-robed figures below. Framed by bands of ornament, the whole cupola becomes an image of heaven opening above the worshipper.
facts: The church takes its popular name, 'Church under the Tree', from its setting in the Ihlara gorge; it is also called the Church of Daniel after a painting of Daniel between the lions facing the entrance.
English Wikipedia describes the Ascension in the cupola as pre-Iconoclast, while other sources date the paintings to the 9th–11th centuries; their unusual, schematic style makes them hard to date.
cur:monumental2-agacalti-ascension.notes: Date disputed: proposals range from the 7th century (pre-Iconoclast) to the 10th–11th century.
